https://www.politico.eu/article/maxi-mer.text: PARIS — French schools are getting torched. The far right’s brightest star is fighting for his political life after being accused of antisemitic remarks. And economic indicators are flashing bright red to warn of a potential sovereign debt disaster in the country. The crises that have rocked France in recent days are exacerbating partisan cleavages in the country’s increasingly no-holds-barred presidential campaign. In the words of one government adviser: “It’s the maxi merde .” Advertisement Advertisement Though that individual, who was granted anonymity to candidly discuss the current situation, was only referring to the increasingly violent demonstrations outside secondary schools and the government’s slow-footed response to them, it’s a sentiment likely shared by French voters after a week of particularly bleak headlines. If there are political winners, it’s not immediately clear who they are. Establishment candidates and moderate voices are still struggling to seize the narrative from far-right presidential front-runner Marine Le Pen and her surging far-left challenger Jean-Luc Mélenchon — both of whom want to fundamentally reshape France and its relationship with Europe. A survey by pollster Odoxa this week found that the French disapprove of the government’s handling of the student school protests, but they also disapprove of Mélenchon and his far-left party France Unbowed’s involvement. Mélenchon and his allies have supported the demonstrators and joined them outside schools, saying they were there to show support and protect minors from confrontations with police. But the government and France Unbowed’s political opponents accuse them of fanning the flames of violence — allegations they deny. “There’s a battle over the narrative” between the political extremes, a Socialist Party adviser said. Whatever the case, the week’s crises are showing just how nasty the campaign can get with two populist candidates unafraid to stoke partisan divisions leading the polls. Advertisement Advertisement Diversion tactics The French government has tried to get a grip on the unravelling protests, holding a crisis meeting Thursday and meeting youth representatives on Friday. “Lecornu is always running behind the crises, he’s always reacting,” said a centrist adviser. Le Pen, however, blamed agitators for stirring up violence at the protests and accused France Unbowed of “giving a helping hand” to “agents of chaos and insurrection.” For her National Rally party, the crisis is a useful opportunity to try to convince voters that her party is the best choice for those concerned with public safety. “We have a government that is incapable of maintaining public order and a left that is stoking the fire,” said National Rally MP Laurent Jacobelli in an interview with POLITICO. “We are the only legitimate ones when it comes to [security],” he added. Advertisement Advertisement But the unrest is also a useful distraction for Le Pen as her party president and heir apparent, Jordan Bardella, tries to bat down allegations published Monday by investigative outlet Mediapart that he sent antisemitic messages on Facebook Messenger when he was a 17-year-old activist. Bardella vehemently denied the allegations and vowed to sue Mediapart, but the website on Thursday published another story outlining how it verified the claims, which included screenshots and conversation data downloaded directly from Meta with the help of their sources. Bardella was tipped to become Le Pen’s prime minister if she came to power, but his future appears to hang on a thread. “Do we need to unplug him? It’s Marine’s decision,” said a National Rally elected representative. “It all depends on whether the proof is serious.” But Bardella is no small player, and the National Rally’s opponents are hoping that the fallout of his possible resignation would damage Le Pen’s campaign durably. Budget trouble All of this comes just hours after Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s minority government introduced a 2027 budget with €43 billion worth of savings designed to reassure markets fretting about France’s massive debt and a stubbornly high budget deficit. Advertisement Advertisement But without a parliamentary majority, getting lawmakers to agree to painful cuts will be tough, even if the specter of a potential financial crisis is starting to loom large. Borrowing cost have reached their highest levels since 2008 and the spread between French 10-year bonds and German ones — an indicator that measures investors’ appetite to hold French debt over more traditionally stable German debt — shot above 150 basis points on Friday, a level not seen in years. One lawmaker from President Emmanuel Macron’s party Renaissance said he doesn’t see how the presidential hopefuls from the political center — former PMs Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal — will be spared the fallout. “Every minute spent on the budget is a minute spent staring at our incapacity to get ourselves out of the mess,” the MP said. Meanwhile, Mélenchon has called for his party officials to join more protests planned next Tuesday and protect pupils against alleged police violence. That could propel him to center stage, but it could also backfire if he is seen as taking part in the unrest. Centrist MEP Sandro Gozi said the allegations against Bardella and the far left’s attitude to the protests “complicate the normalization strategy of the two sides.” Advertisement Advertisement “Both Le Pen and Mélenchon are extremists who are far from fundamental Republican and European values,” Gozi said. But as Macron’s term winds down, a sense is taking hold that France has been mismanaged and that parts of the country are falling apart. It’s a perception any would-be successor with links to the current president will struggle to combat on the campaign trail. Elisa Bertholomey and Sarah Paillou contributed reporting.

The Spectre of ‘Pro-Russian Sentiment’: Decoding Donald Tusk’s Political Anxiety 9 October 2025 A rethinking of Polish-Ukrainian relations and a reassessment of Ukraine’s role in Polish interests are entirely possible. However, this process will likely unfold in an atmosphere of emotional tension, amid a “hunt for pro-Russian witches” and increasingly heated debates over historical memory, writes Anton Bespalov , Programme Director of the Valdai Discussion Club. In mid-September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted on the social media platform X about a “growing wave of pro-Russian sentiment and hostility toward fighting Ukraine.” Accusations of holding “pro-Russian” positions are a standard rhetorical trope in Polish domestic politics; Tusk himself has been labelled “the most pro-Russian politician since 1989” by his opponents. However, in this instance, he is referring to something different: an alleged trend that has supposedly permeated all of Polish society. But is this true? The CBOS Public Opinion Research Centre’s 2025 data, part of its-decades-long study of Polish attitudes, shows a slight improvement in views toward Russians. The proportion of respondents with a negative attitude fell from 76% in 2024 to 72%, while those sympathetic to Russians increased from 6% in 2023 to 8%. This comes after the 2023 survey found an all-time low, with a record 82% of Poles expressing a negative attitude toward Russians – the highest figure for any nation in the history of the research. These surveys, however, do not account for the nuanced distinction sometimes made in Polish discourse between the Russian people and the Russian state. Were this distinction factored in, the recorded hostility would almost certainly be greater and its variations more stable. Since a minor drop from an extremely high level of negativity cannot be considered a radical shift in public opinion, other factors must be at play. Tusk’s statement came just days after unidentified drones entered Polish airspace. Hours after the incident, the research centre Res Futura published an analysis of social media comments on the event. The findings revealed that 38% of users blamed Ukraine for the drones’ arrival, 34% blamed Russia, 15% the Polish government, 8% the media, and 5% the West. These results shocked Polish commentators, some of whom declared that Poland was “losing the information war with Russia.” This concern is amplified by former President Duda’s recent statement regarding the 2022 Przewodów tragedy, where a Ukrainian missile killed two civilians. Duda claims that Zelensky then attempted to leverage the incident by pressuring Warsaw to falsely blame Russia, aiming to draw Poland into the war. Although Poland has provided extensive support to Ukraine, the majority of Poles firmly reject any direct involvement in the war. This, however, is just one reason for shifting perceptions. A more critical factor is the presence of 1.5 million Ukrainian citizens, including a million refugees. A growing segment of Polish society believes these refugees are receiving undue advantages, such as the controversial “800 plus” benefit, fostering a sense that Poles are becoming “second-class citizens in their own country.” This list of irritants is compounded by historical disputes, particularly regarding the 1943 Volhynia Massacre and the modern glorification of Ukrainian nationalist figures who collaborated with the Nazis. The Polish political elite is highly sensitive to these issues; anti-Ukrainian narratives featured to varying degrees in the campaigns of all candidates during the recent presidential election . In essence, the “growing pro-Russian sentiment” described by Tusk is less an embrace of Russia and more a rise in anti-Ukrainian sentiment. More critically, it represents the increasing vocalization of viewpoints that align with notorious “Kremlin narratives.” In modern Poland – as across much of Europe – echoing these narratives is the ultimate political sin, even when they reflect objective reality. The ruling class’s reaction has been to consistently accuse its opponents of promoting a Russian agenda, thereby igniting a new round of the internal “Polish-Polish war.” Historical data on Polish attitudes reveals a curious pattern: prior to 2004, both Russians and Ukrainians received similarly low favourability ratings, with Ukrainians sometimes ranking lower than Russians. This distinction in attitude had different sources. Animosity toward Russians was driven largely by historical grievances and media narratives, whereas negative views of Ukrainians were also fuelled by direct, often contentious, interactions stemming from labour migration. Polish sympathy for Ukrainians surged in 2004 due to the Orange Revolution’s impact on Polish self-awareness. After this euphoria subsided, attitudes stabilized. For instance, in 2012, positive and negative ratings for Russians and Ukrainians were nearly identical (around 33% positive/negative for each). A decisive shift came in 2014-15 revealing rising antipathy toward Russians and growing sympathy for Ukrainians. This trend culminated explosively in 2023 with negative attitudes toward Russians skyrocketing from 38% to a record 82%, while positive attitudes toward Ukrainians peaked at 51%, and negative attitudes fell to a historic low of 17%. As in 2004, the surge in pro-Ukrainian sentiment during 2022-23 was deeply tied to the war’s impact on Polish national self-assertion. This was perfectly captured in President Andrzej Duda’s May 2022 speech to the Verkhovna Rada, which wove together three key themes: first, the opportunity to wage a seemingly successful proxy war against Russia; second, the validation of Poland’s role as an “unheard Cassandra,” whose long-standing warnings about “Russian imperialism” were finally being proven right; and third, the image of Poland as a magnanimous benefactor, providing both refuge and a steadfast commitment to Ukraine’s European future. The events of subsequent years, however, have profoundly altered both the image of Ukraine and Polish expectations. This shift was starkly illustrated in July 2025, when the same Duda sharply criticized Kiev’s attitude toward military aid, threatening to close the critical airfield in Rzeszów if Ukrainians and their Western allies continued to treat it as “their own property.” Both Polish society and its political elite are undergoing a volatile emotional swing over Ukraine. This stems from a fundamental tension: the principles of Poland’s post-1989 policy, conceptually shared across the political spectrum, are in a state of traumatic collision with reality. Rooted in the neo-Jagiellonian vision of Giedroyc and Mieroszewski, this doctrine posits an independent Ukraine as a fundamental Polish national interest. Yet reality has consistently defied Polish expectations – from the failure of rapid democratization after the Orange Revolution to the stalled victory over Russia in 2022. Most critically, Ukraine has persistently rejected the tacitly offered role of junior partner in the Polish-Ukrainian tandem. The current conflict represents the most complex test in over thirty years for the conceptual foundations of Polish eastern policy. While Russia will undoubtedly remain the primary geopolitical adversary in the Polish consciousness – ensuring that “pro-Russian sentiment” remains a potent bogeyman in domestic politics – a rethinking of Polish-Ukrainian relations is now entirely possible. Any such reassessment of Ukraine’s role in Polish interests, however, will inevitably unfold in an atmosphere of intense emotional tension, marked by a hunt for “pro-Russian witches” and increasingly heated debates over historical memory. https://valdaiclub.com/a/highlights/the-spectre-of-pro-russian-sentiment-decoding? Some 2,800 troops from 10 European countries will this month stage in Poland the first exercise of a new multinational force in support of Ukraine , London and Paris said on Tuesday. Led by France and the UK, the Multinational Force – Ukraine (MNF-U) has no offensive mission and is only to be deployed once a ceasefire is agreed to end the war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The force, which was set up in 2025 and already has an operational headquarters in Paris, is not a NATO operation and has little US involvement. It aims to support the Ukrainian armed forces, ensure security in Ukrainian skies and allow economic activity to resume in the Black Sea. But the extent and duration of the exercise, dubbed Koalicja ("Coalition" in Polish), risks antagonising Russia , with Moscow still showing little appetite to settle for peace. "The exercise will allow the testing of the speed and efficiency at which several nations can deploy forces on land, sea and air to support Ukraine once hostilities have finished," said the joint statement released by the French defence ministry. "This isn't a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops," UK Defence Minister Wes Streeting was quoted as saying in the UK statement. The exercise is scheduled to last from November 9 to 22 in southeast Poland not far from the Ukrainian border, involving 2,800 troops. The largest contingent of 1,100 troops will come from France , with the UK deploying 300 soldiers. The first exercise for the coalition force is "a key milestone, as it will serve as a concrete demonstration of the MNF-U's ability to be deployed as soon as hostilities have ended," said French General Armel Dirou, who will co-lead the exercise alongside Britain's Lieutenant General Tom Bateman. It will involve troops from Belgium , Estonia, Germany , France, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain , Sweden and the UK in air and land operations around the town of Nowa Deba, some 100 kilometres (62 miles) west of the Ukrainian border, the joint statement said. Meanwhile, a maritime simulation will be led by Turkey from Istanbul to test preparedness for eventual mine-clearing operations in the Black Sea. Turkish troops will not be involved in the land exercise in Poland, it added. Bateman emphasised that the force is not a "peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring mission". "It is not designed for offensive operations.
